{{short description|American theoretical particle physicist|bot=PearBOT 5}}
[[File:Thomas Appelquist.jpg|thumb|Thomas Appelquist, Eugene Higgins Professor of Physics, Yale University]]
'''Thomas William Appelquist''' (born 1941) is an American [[Theoretical physics|theoretical]] [[particle physics|particle physicist]] who is the [[Eugene Higgins]] Professor of Physics Emeritus at [[Yale University]].<ref>{{citation |url=http://physics.yale.edu/people/thomas-appelquist |title=Thomas Appelquist |publisher=[[Yale University]]}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
Appelquist was born in Emmetsburg, Iowa and grew up in Indiana. He received his bachelor's degree from [[Benedictine University|Illinois Benedictine College]] and his Ph.D. in 1968 from [[Cornell University]] under [[Donald R. Yennie]] with thesis ''Parametric Representations of Renormalized Feynman Amplitudes''.<ref>[http://cornell.worldcat.org/title/parametric-representations-of-renormalized-feynman-amplitudes/oclc/63221018 dissertation oclc, Cornell U. Library]</ref> Following a postdoctoral appointment at the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]], he joined the faculty at [[Harvard University]] in 1970, where he collaborated with [[H. David Politzer]] on [[charmonium]]. In 1975, he moved to [[Yale University|Yale]] and was appointed professor of physics in 1976.

At Yale, he served as chair of the Department of Physics (1983–1989), director of the division of physical sciences and engineering (1990–1993), and dean of the [[Yale Graduate School of Arts and Sciences|Graduate School]] (1993–1998). In 1991, he was named Eugene Higgins Professor of Physics.

== Research ==

=== Charmonium ===
In 1974, Appelquist and [[H. David Politzer|Politzer]] predicted the existence of narrow bound states of a [[charm quark]] and charm antiquark, which they named "[[charmonium]]" by analogy with [[positronium]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Appelquist |first1=Thomas |last2=Politzer |first2=H. David |title=Heavy Quarks and e<sup>+</sup>e<sup>−</sup> Annihilation |journal=[[Physical Review Letters]] |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=43–45 |year=1975 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.34.43 |bibcode=1975PhRvL..34...43A}}</ref> They argued that [[asymptotic freedom]] renders the strong force between heavy quarks Coulomb-like at the relevant distance scales, leading to a positronium-like spectrum with narrow widths. Their paper was in preparation when the [[J/psi meson|J/ψ]] was discovered in November 1974 at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory|Brookhaven]] and [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|SLAC]]. With [[Alvaro de Rújula]], Politzer, and [[Sheldon Glashow]], Appelquist subsequently predicted the P-wave charmonium states observed in radiative decays of the ψ'.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Appelquist |first1=T. |last2=De Rújula |first2=A. |last3=Politzer |first3=H. D. |last4=Glashow |first4=S. L. |title=Spectroscopy of the New Mesons |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=34 |issue=6 |pages=365–368 |year=1975 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.34.365 |bibcode=1975PhRvL..34..365A}}</ref>

=== Decoupling theorem ===
With James Carazzone, Appelquist proved the [[decoupling theorem]] in [[quantum field theory]], showing that in a renormalizable theory the effects of heavy particles on low-energy physics are suppressed by inverse powers of the heavy mass and can be absorbed into renormalized parameters of the low-energy theory.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Appelquist |first1=T. |last2=Carazzone |first2=J. |title=Infrared singularities and massive fields |journal=[[Physical Review D]] |volume=11 |issue=10 |pages=2856–2861 |year=1975 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.11.2856 |bibcode=1975PhRvD..11.2856A}}</ref> The Appelquist–Carazzone decoupling theorem is a foundational result in the [[effective field theory]] approach to particle physics.

=== Beyond the Standard Model ===
Appelquist has made several influential contributions to physics beyond the [[Standard Model]]. With collaborators, he developed the [[electroweak interaction|electroweak]] [[chiral perturbation theory|chiral Lagrangian]] framework for parametrizing deviations from the Standard Model in the symmetry-breaking sector. He proposed [[walking technicolor]] theories, in which the gauge coupling evolves slowly ("walks") over a wide range of energy scales, addressing phenomenological challenges of earlier [[technicolor (physics)|technicolor]] models.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Appelquist |first1=Thomas |last2=Karabali |first2=Dimitra |last3=Wijewardhana |first3=L.C.R. |title=Chiral Hierarchies and the Flavor Changing Neutral Current Problem in Technicolor |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=57 |issue=8 |pages=957–960 |year=1986 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.57.957 |bibcode=1986PhRvL..57..957A |pmid=10034202}}</ref>

With Hsin-Chia Cheng and Bogdan Dobrescu, he introduced the concept of [[universal extra dimensions]], in which all Standard Model fields propagate in compact extra dimensions, leading to a distinctive spectrum of [[Kaluza–Klein theory|Kaluza–Klein]] excitations and a natural [[dark matter]] candidate.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Appelquist |first1=Thomas |last2=Cheng |first2=Hsin-Chia |last3=Dobrescu |first3=Bogdan A. |title=Bounds on universal extra dimensions |journal=Physical Review D |volume=64 |issue=3 |article-number=035002 |year=2001 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.64.035002 |arxiv=hep-ph/0012100 |bibcode=2001PhRvD..64c5002A}}</ref>

=== Lattice strong dynamics ===
Appelquist is a founding member of the Lattice Strong Dynamics (LSD) Collaboration, which uses [[lattice gauge theory]] simulations to study strongly coupled gauge theories relevant to electroweak symmetry breaking and composite dark matter. His recent work has focused on effective field theories with approximate conformal symmetry and an associated [[dilaton]], motivated by lattice studies of near-conformal gauge theories.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Appelquist |first1=Thomas |last2=Ingoldby |first2=James |last3=Piai |first3=Maurizio |title=Dilaton EFT framework for lattice data |journal=[[Journal of High Energy Physics]] |volume=2017 |issue=7 |page=035 |year=2017 |doi=10.1007/JHEP07(2017)035 |arxiv=1702.04410 |bibcode=2017JHEP...07..035A}}</ref>

== Honors and service ==
He is a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (elected 1984),<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1984&unit_id=&institution=Yale+University}} (search on year=1984 and institution=Yale University)</ref> a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (elected 1993), and the recipient of a Senior U.S. Scientist Award from the [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation]]. In 1997, he was awarded the [[Sakurai Prize|J. J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics]] of the American Physical Society for his work on charmonium and the decoupling of heavy particles.<ref>{{citation |url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Appelquist&first_nm=Thomas&year=1997 |title=1997 J.J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics Recipient |publisher=[[American Physical Society]]}}</ref>

He served as President (1993–1996) and Chair of the Board (2001–2006) of the [[Aspen Center for Physics]]. He was a member of the Scientific Policy Committee of the [[Superconducting Super Collider]] Laboratory (1989–1993) and chaired the Science Council of [[Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility|Jefferson National Laboratory]] (2007–2017). He chaired the National Research Council committee that produced the survey ''Physics in a New Era'' (1999–2001). He has served on advisory committees for the [[National Science Foundation]], the [[United States Department of Energy|Department of Energy]], and the American Physical Society. At Yale, he served on the faculty/trustee Presidential Search Committee during the 1992–1993 academic year.
